passage: Jaya started selling her mother's mango pickle from a stall at the Tuesday market in Ratnagiri. Customers loved it, so she borrowed from her savings group, bought jars and printed labels. Anirban, a friend who ran a mobile repair shop, helped her set up orders over a chat app. For eight months it grew. Then mango prices doubled after a bad season, and a bigger brand cut its price. By winter Jaya was losing money on every jar. She cried in the storeroom, then sat down with Anirban and her notebook. They wrote down what had worked: loyal customers, the recipe, the market stall. What hadn't: no plan for bad seasons. She closed the business in March, repaid the group and kept the customer list.

qa.q: What did Jaya first sell at the Tuesday market?
qa.a: She sold her mother's mango pickle.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when she was losing money, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was heartbroken and stressed; she cried in the storeroom before facing the numbers.

qa.q: What did Jaya do well in shutting the business down?
qa.a: She reviewed what worked and what didn't, repaid her savings group and kept the customer list for the future.

qa.q: How might Jaya's savings group see her after she repaid them?
qa.a: They would likely trust her more, seeing that she handled failure honestly and kept her word.

grounding: Shows a young woman taking a small venture from idea to customers and learning from its closure.

passage: Astrid and Thabo met at a coding bootcamp in Cape Town and spent a year building an app to help small bakeries track orders. They pitched to eleven investors. Ten said no. One asked sharp questions about how many bakeries actually paid. Astrid admitted: four. That night Thabo wanted to quit. Astrid wanted to keep going. They argued on the balcony until two in the morning. The next week, instead of building features, they visited thirty bakeries and asked what really wasted their time. Most said it wasn't orders, it was staff schedules. It hurt to throw away months of work. But they rebuilt around scheduling, and six months later twenty bakeries were paying. They still hadn't raised money. They were earning it instead.

qa.q: How many investors did Astrid and Thabo pitch to?
qa.a: They pitched to eleven investors.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when Thabo wanted to quit?
qa.a: Thabo felt discouraged and worn out after so many rejections and the admission that only four bakeries paid.

qa.q: What turned things around for their venture?
qa.a: Talking directly to thirty bakeries to find their real problem, then rebuilding the product around it.

qa.q: How might the bakery owners have seen being asked about their problems?
qa.a: They probably felt listened to, which made them more likely to pay for a tool that fit their real needs. 🙂

grounding: Shows two young founders facing rejection and redesigning their venture around what customers really needed.

passage: At the college incubator in Kochi, Jomon's desk had a sign: 'Farm-to-canteen, fresh daily.' His venture supplied vegetables from nearby farms to three hostel canteens. The incubator mentor, Lokesh, asked him to present his numbers at the monthly review. Jomon's hands were shaking when he showed the slide. Spoilage was eating most of his profit. Two canteens paid late. "I think I should shut it," he said quietly. Lokesh didn't rush to comfort him. He asked, "What did you learn that the next version needs?" Jomon listed three things: cold storage, payment terms in writing, and fewer customers who pay reliably. He closed the venture that term. The next year he helped a new student team avoid the same mistakes.

qa.q: How many hostel canteens did Jomon's venture supply?
qa.a: It supplied three hostel canteens.

qa.q: Why were Jomon's hands shaking during his presentation?
qa.a: He was nervous and probably ashamed to show that his venture was losing money.

qa.q: How did Lokesh's question help Jomon?
qa.a: It turned a painful failure into a list of lessons, so the closure became useful rather than only a loss.

qa.q: How might the new student team see Jomon's past failure?
qa.a: They would see it as valuable experience that could save them from making the same mistakes.

grounding: Shows a young founder at an incubator shutting down a venture and turning its failure into lessons.

passage:
Dear Nirmala ma'am,
I wanted you to hear it from me first: we're shutting down the millet-snack venture at the end of this month. Two years ago you told me to sell a hundred packets before building anything bigger, and I'm glad I listened; it's why the loss is small. We did reach real customers, around four hundred regulars in Ludhiana and Chandigarh, and the money from my uncle's friend kept us going for eighteen months. But our cost per packet never came down enough, and the big stores wanted margins we couldn't give. I cried for two days, honestly. Then I wrote down everything I'd do differently: price for profit from the first batch, talk to store buyers before designing packaging. I'll repay our investor as much as I can and take a job for a while. I'm not done with building things.
Gratefully,
Gurpreet

qa.q: How many regular customers did Gurpreet's venture reach?
qa.a: Around four hundred regulars in Ludhiana and Chandigarh.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel about shutting down, and what shows it?
qa.a: Deeply sad, since Gurpreet cried for two days, but also determined, as the line 'I'm not done with building things' shows.

qa.q: What lessons did Gurpreet take from the shutdown?
qa.a: Price for profit from the first batch, and talk to store buyers early before spending on things like packaging.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sad for Gurpreet but proud that Gurpreet tested small first, learned honestly and still wants to build.

grounding: A letter shows a young founder who reached real customers closing the venture and drawing clear lessons from it.

passage: Anirban, I'm Dolma, and people on your podcast always want the rocket story. Mine's more of a bicycle. I grew up in Kalimpong, and every tourist season the small homestays lost bookings because they weren't online. So at twenty-four I started helping five families put their rooms on a simple website, for a small commission. I took the photos myself on my phone. The first month we got three bookings. Three! I celebrated like it was a hundred. When I went to investors, the first ten said no; one said the market was too small. Honestly, that stung for weeks. Then a small-business programme at a local cooperative bank gave us a modest loan, and two homestay owners became my loudest salespeople. Now we have sixty families. Some months are still scary. But every booking is a real family earning, and that keeps me going.

qa.q: How many bookings did Dolma get in the first month?
qa.a: Three bookings.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when the investors turned Dolma down?
qa.a: Hurt; the rejections, especially being told the market was too small, stung for weeks.

qa.q: What helped Dolma's venture grow despite the investor rejections?
qa.a: Starting small with real customers, finding a modest loan through a local programme, and letting happy homestay owners spread the word.

qa.q: How might the homestay families see Dolma's work?
qa.a: As practical help that brings real bookings and income, which is why two of them became Dolma's loudest salespeople 🙂

grounding: A young founder describes taking a small venture from idea to paying customers and finding funding after rejections.

passage: I'm Gurleen, and I rented the desk next to Deepak's at a co-working space in Indore for the eighteen months his startup lived. It sold refurbished tablets to small private schools. I watched him call forty schools in the first month and sign three. I watched the day an investor said yes, and the day, a year later, the next round fell through. He didn't shout. He sat very still for a long time. Then he did something I didn't expect: he called every one of his twenty-two customer schools himself, told them the truth, and arranged for a local repair shop to handle their warranties. On his last day he pinned a sheet above his desk titled "What I got wrong": priced too low, hired before revenue, ignored the months when school budgets freeze. I don't know if he was heartbroken. He took the sheet with him.

qa.q: How many customer schools did Deepak have at the end?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: What might Deepak have been feeling when he sat very still after the funding fell through?
qa.a: Deepak was probably shocked and deeply disappointed, though Gurleen can only guess from his stillness.

qa.q: What did Deepak handle responsibly during the shutdown?
qa.a: He told every customer the truth himself, arranged warranty support, and wrote down what he got wrong so he could learn from it.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Deepak's shutdown from the next desk?
qa.a: Gurleen watched closely and seems to respect how honestly he closed, while admitting not knowing how heartbroken he was.

grounding: A desk neighbour observes a young founder take a venture to customers and then shut it down honestly, noting lessons.

passage:
February. Baljeet quit her bank job to sell her Bebe's mango and lime pickles online. She had jars, labels and a website, and after two weeks, four orders, all from cousins.
April. Yusuf, a friend who ran a small spice shop in Ludhiana, tasted a jar and said, "It's good. But who is it for?" Baljeet didn't know. So she stopped designing labels and started standing at Sunday markets with free tasting spoons, asking people what they would buy and why. She learned that office workers wanted small jars, not big ones, and hated oily lids.
August. She relaunched with small leak-proof jars and a tiffin-sized pack. Yusuf stocked twenty in his shop. An investor offered money for a big share; she read the terms with her CA and said no, for now. That month, for the first time, strangers outnumbered cousins in her orders.

qa.q: How many orders did Baljeet get after two weeks?
qa.a: Four orders, all from cousins.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling when Yusuf asked who the pickles were for?
qa.a: Baljeet probably felt unsettled and a bit embarrassed, realising she didn't know her customer.

qa.q: What changed when Baljeet went to the Sunday markets?
qa.a: Talking to real buyers showed they wanted small, leak-proof jars, so she relaunched the product to fit them.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Baljeet's progress by August?
qa.a: Yusuf seems to believe in it, stocking twenty jars, and may feel proud that his blunt question helped.

grounding: Over months, a young woman takes a pickle venture from friends-only orders to real customers by learning what buyers need.

passage: Yamini, before you sign that shop lease, let your Nazia Khala tell you about the boutique I opened at twenty-five in Aminabad. I had the prettiest shop in the lane: mirror work, lights, a name board painted by hand. I spent everything on how it looked before I knew who would walk in. For six months, people admired the window and walked on. I borrowed from my brother to pay rent, and then again. I remember counting the drawer every night, eighty rupees, a hundred and twenty, and telling Ammi it was fine. The turning point was the day I closed. I sat with a notebook and wrote: I never asked a single customer what they wanted. Two years later I started again, from home, stitching blouses for women in our mohalla who told me exactly what they needed. That one lasted twenty years. So talk to your customers before your carpenter, Yamini.

qa.q: Where did Nazia open her boutique?
qa.a: In Aminabad.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling while telling Ammi it was fine?
qa.a: Nazia felt anxious and ashamed, hiding the failing shop's struggle from her mother.

qa.q: What was Nazia's turning point, and how did it shape her second business?
qa.a: Realising that not one customer had been asked what they wanted; the second business started from what women in the mohalla said they needed.

qa.q: How might Nazia's brother have felt lending money twice?
qa.a: Her brother was probably worried about her and the shop, and perhaps uneasy lending again, though he helped anyway.

grounding: An aunt tells a young woman how her first boutique failed for lack of customers and what she learned for her lasting venture.

passage:
The power went out in the co-working space ten minutes before Vandana's pitch, and her laptop battery showed four percent.

She had one chance with Anirban, an angel investor who had flown in for the day. No slides now. She pulled out the printed order sheets from her millet-snack stall: 312 customers in six months, 140 of them buying again.

"I started with a stall outside a school," she said, holding up a packet. "Parents asked for less sugar, so I changed the recipe twice."

Anirban read the sheets by his phone torch. "Why haven't shops picked you up?"

"Two tried. I couldn't keep up with packaging."

He didn't invest. But he said, "Your repeat numbers are real. Fix supply, then call me."

Walking home in the rain, Vandana was disappointed and oddly light. She wrote "supply first" on her wrist in pen.

qa.q: How many of Vandana's customers were buying again?
qa.a: 140 of the 312 customers were buying again.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel after Anirban declined to invest?
qa.a: Vandana was disappointed, but also oddly light, because his feedback told her exactly what to fix next.

qa.q: What could Vandana do next, based on the pitch?
qa.a: She could sort out packaging and supply so shops can stock her snacks, then go back to Anirban with those results.

qa.q: How might Anirban see Vandana after the pitch without slides?
qa.a: Anirban was impressed by her real customer numbers and her calm under pressure, even if the business was not ready for his money yet.

grounding: A young founder pitches her snack venture to an investor during a power cut, showing real customers and learning what to fix before funding.

passage:
Suraj pinned the last invoice to the corkboard in their tiny office above a Pune sweet shop and sat down heavily.

Eighteen months ago, he and Tushar had started a doorstep bicycle-repair service. Students loved it. The trouble was that students also moved away every summer, and the mechanics cost more than the bookings brought in.

"We shut it on the 30th," Tushar said quietly. "We agreed."

"I know." Suraj stared at the board. "I keep thinking if we'd just raised money in March..."

"We'd have lost someone else's money too."

That evening, instead of drinking chai in silence, they opened a shared document titled "What we'd do differently." Tushar typed: talk to fifty customers before building anything. Suraj added: check who stays in the city. They wrote for two hours.

Before leaving, Suraj rang each of their four mechanics himself, thanking them and offering references.

qa.q: What kind of service did Suraj and Tushar start?
qa.a: They started a doorstep bicycle-repair service.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stared at the corkboard?
qa.a: Suraj felt heavy with regret and disappointment, still wondering whether raising money in March could have saved the business.

qa.q: Which choice after the shutdown was wise, and why?
qa.a: Writing down what they would do differently turned the failure into lessons, and calling the mechanics kept trust and respect intact.

qa.q: How might the four mechanics feel about the shutdown?
qa.a: They would be worried about losing work, but Suraj's personal call and offer of references would help them feel respected rather than dropped.

grounding: Two young founders close a venture that did not work, reflect on why, and learn from the shutdown while treating their workers fairly.

passage:
"Forty regular customers," Jaya said, tapping the notebook. "Forty! From one building's group chat."

"Forty tiffins a day from my mother's kitchen," Ankita said, laughing. "My back knows."

"So now what? My uncle says he'll put in money if we open a proper kitchen."

Ankita put down the ladle. "And if we fail, every Diwali lunch becomes very awkward."

Jaya grinned, then sobered. "Seriously. Three office canteens asked for trial orders. We can't cook that much in your mother's kitchen."

"Then let's do the trials first. Borrow a kitchen for two weeks. If the canteens reorder, we talk to your uncle with real numbers, and a written agreement."

"And if they don't?"

"Then we're still a tiffin service with forty happy customers. That's not nothing."

Jaya wrote TRIALS FIRST in big letters and circled it.

qa.q: How many office canteens asked for trial orders?
qa.a: Three office canteens asked for trial orders.

qa.q: Why did Jaya sober up after grinning?
qa.a: Jaya felt worried about growing too fast, since their home kitchen could not handle the canteen orders, and family money could be risked carelessly.

qa.q: What plan did Ankita suggest, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Ankita suggested testing with borrowed kitchen space first and only approaching the uncle with real reorder numbers and a written agreement, which lowers the risk to family ties.

qa.q: How might Jaya's uncle see the plan to wait?
qa.a: The uncle might feel slightly put off at first, but would probably respect being approached later with real numbers and a clear written agreement.

grounding: Two young co-founders with their first customers decide to test demand before taking family money, keeping the venture and relationships safe.

passage:
Our tiffin start-up lasted fourteen months. My co-founder Pema and I started it at twenty-four: home-style lunches for office workers in Pune, cooked by women from our neighbourhood.
The first three months were magic. We had two hundred customers from a word-of-mouth list and a spreadsheet. An investor gave us a small amount after one meeting. We hired, bought a van, rented a kitchen.
Then offices went hybrid. Orders halved in six weeks. We kept spending as if they'd come back. I stopped sleeping. My mother kept asking, "Beta, are you eating?"
In month thirteen, Pema said it first: "We have to shut it down properly." We paid every cook, returned what we could, and wrote to each customer.
I'm Sahil. It hurt like a breakup. But I learned more in those fourteen months than in college: test before you spend, watch your cash every week, and end honestly.

qa.q: How long did the tiffin start-up last?
qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when orders halved?
qa.a: Sahil felt anxious and overwhelmed, to the point of not sleeping.

qa.q: What lessons from Sahil's failure could help another founder?
qa.a: Test demand before spending, track cash weekly, and when it's over, shut down honestly by paying people and telling customers.

qa.q: How might the cooks have felt about the way the venture ended?
qa.a: The cooks were probably sad to lose the work but respected being paid in full and told honestly.

grounding: Shows a young founder taking a venture from idea to customers and learning from its shutdown.

passage:
Incubator mentor's note. Kavitha.
Salma, 25, came to us with handloom saris from weavers in her mother's village. She had passion and no customers.
I asked her to sell twenty saris before we talked about funding. She put them on a stall at a Sunday market in Hyderabad, then at two office exhibitions. She sold fourteen, and learned that younger buyers wanted lighter cotton, not heavy silk.
She pitched to three investors. All said no, one rather rudely. She came to my office red-eyed. We went through each rejection: two said her costs were unclear. She rebuilt her numbers with the weavers, line by line.
She still hasn't raised money. But she has forty repeat customers and a small order from a boutique. I've told her: revenue from customers is also funding. She's planning a second collection in cotton.

qa.q: How many saris did Salma sell out of twenty?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: How did Salma feel after the investor rejections?
qa.a: Salma was upset and discouraged, arriving at the office red-eyed.

qa.q: What did Kavitha's approach teach Salma about launching a venture?
qa.a: Selling to real customers first revealed what buyers wanted, and studying rejections showed her the cost figures needed fixing.

qa.q: How might the weavers see Salma's progress?
qa.a: The weavers probably feel hopeful and more secure, with repeat customers and a boutique order bringing steady work.

grounding: Illustrates a young entrepreneur finding first customers, facing fundraising rejection and learning from it.

passage:
Friday night
Tanvir writing. Today Kashish and I told our team of six that the app is shutting down. Two years. Three pivots. No more money.
I'd rehearsed it all week. I still couldn't get through the first sentence without my voice cracking. Kashish took over and explained: last pay plus one extra month, reference letters, and our help finding their next jobs.
Nobody shouted. Sonal, our designer, hugged us both. That almost made it worse.
What went wrong? We built for a year before talking to real users. We raised money before we knew anyone would pay. We hired too fast.
What went right? We were honest with the team when things got bad. We didn't hide it from investors.
I feel like a failure tonight. Kashish says we are founders who failed once, which is different. I'm going to sleep and try to believe that.

qa.q: How many people were in the team?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling while telling the team?
qa.a: Tanvir felt heartbroken and ashamed, voice cracking, and feels like a failure tonight.

qa.q: What did Tanvir and Kashish handle well in the shutdown?
qa.a: They told the team honestly, paid an extra month, offered references and job help, and kept investors informed.

qa.q: How might Sonal have felt hugging the founders?
qa.a: Sonal was probably sad about losing the job but warm and grateful for how honestly they'd treated the team.

grounding: Shows young founders shutting down a venture and reflecting honestly on what went wrong and right.
